summary: On the flagged day, China announced retaliatory tariffs of 25% on 106 U.S. product lines — explicitly including soybeans and Boeing aircraft — in response to a prior U.S. threat of tariffs covering up to $50 billion of Chinese goods. This is a direct, tit-for-tat escalation between the world's two largest economies naming specific large-cap exporters and agricultural commodities, and it is the only item in the window with clear, immediate implications for asset prices.
mechanism: Announced retaliatory tariffs on named sectors force repricing of earnings expectations for exporters (aircraft, agriculture) and of global supply-chain risk generally, while the tit-for-tat pattern raises uncertainty about the range of possible outcomes — both of which widen expected return distributions and lift realised and implied volatility.

claims.claim: China threatened 25% tariffs on 106 U.S. product categories, including soybeans and Boeing aircraft, on the final day of the window.
The Chinese measure was framed as a reaction to a previously announced U.S. threat of tariffs worth up to $50 billion.
Trade policy was an active theme earlier in the window, with the United States and South Korea reaching agreements on trade and steel tariffs.
A U.S. fiscal risk was removed earlier in the window when a $1.3 trillion omnibus spending bill was signed, averting a government shutdown for a defined period.
Separately on the flagged day, lawyers for the U.S. President were told by the special counsel that the President is considered more than a witness but is not under criminal investigation.
Diplomatic tension between Russia and Western states continued through the window, including reciprocal consulate closures and the expulsion of 60 U.S. diplomats from Russia.
Security-related headlines with potential commodity relevance appeared late in the window, including a reported repelled attack on a Saudi-flagged oil tanker in the Red Sea.

competing_explanation: Two weaker alternatives exist. First, the political/legal news concerning the U.S. presidency on the same day could move risk sentiment, though the item as reported is arguably de-escalatory. Second, the sustained Russia–West diplomatic confrontation (diplomat expulsions, disputed attribution of a nerve-agent attack, detention of a prominent Russian businessman) plus a reported attack on a Saudi-flagged oil tanker could support a geopolitical-risk reading; but none of these items names an economic transmission channel as concrete as tariffs on specific traded goods.
